plain_english: Remember how long you have been putting these things off. Again and again you have been given the chance, and you have let it pass. It is time for you to understand the true nature of the world you are part of. And understand that Lord who governs the world, from whom you flow like water from a spring. You have only a limited amount of time. If you do not use it to calm the troubles of your soul, time will pass away and you with it. And it will never return.
original_excerpt: Remember how long thou hast already put off these things, and how often a certain day and hour as it were, having been set unto thee by the gods, thou hast neglected it. It is high time for thee to understand the true nature both of the world, whereof thou art a part; and of that Lord and Governor of the world, from whom, as a channel from the spring, thou thyself didst flow: and that there is but a certain limit of time appointed unto thee, which if thou shalt not make use of to calm and allay the many distempers of thy soul, it will pass away and thou with it, and never after return.

plain_english: Make it your constant care as a Roman and as a person to do whatever you're doing with genuine seriousness, natural love, honesty, and fairness. As for all other worries and thoughts — free your mind of them. You can do this if you approach every action as if it were your last. Be free from vanity, from emotional reactions that go against reason, from pretending to be something you're not, from self-centeredness, and from resenting what fate or God has given you. You can see that the things needed for a good life and to live like the gods are not many. The gods ask for nothing more from anyone who keeps to these simple things.
original_excerpt: Let it be thy earnest and incessant care as a Roman and a man to perform whatsoever it is that thou art about, with true and unfeigned gravity, natural affection, freedom and justice: and as for all other cares, and imaginations, how thou mayest ease thy mind of them. Which thou shalt do; if thou shalt go about every action as thy last action, free from all vanity, all passionate and wilful aberration from reason, and from all hypocrisy, and self-love, and dislike of those things, which by the fates or appointment of God have happened unto thee. Thou seest that those things, which for a man to hold on in a prosperous course, and to live a divine life, are requisite and necessary, are not many, for the gods will require no more of any man, that shall but keep and observe these things.

plain_english: Go ahead, soul, go ahead. Abuse yourself and look down on yourself. Soon enough, the time to respect yourself will be over. Every person's happiness comes from within. But look — your life is almost over, and you're still not respecting yourself. You're putting your happiness in what other people think of you.
original_excerpt: Do, soul, do; abuse and contemn thyself; yet a while and the time for thee to respect thyself, will be at an end. Every man's happiness depends from himself, but behold thy life is almost at an end, whiles affording thyself no respect, thou dost make thy happiness to consist in the souls, and conceits of other men.

plain_english: Why should any of these external things disturb you so much? Give yourself time to learn something good, and stop rushing around aimlessly. You must also watch out for another kind of wandering. Some people stay busy with work and effort, but they have no clear purpose to guide their actions and desires.
original_excerpt: Why should any of these things that happen externally, so much distract thee? Give thyself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease roving and wandering to and fro. Thou must also take heed of another kind of wandering, for they are idle in their actions, who toil and labour in this life, and have no certain scope to which to direct all their motions, and desires.

plain_english: A person is rarely unhappy from watching what goes on in someone else's mind. But those who don't pay attention to their own thoughts and feelings, and don't guide them with reason, will definitely be unhappy.
original_excerpt: For not observing the state of another man's soul, scarce was ever any man known to be unhappy. Tell whosoever they be that intend not, and guide not by reason and discretion the motions of their own souls, they must of necessity be unhappy.

plain_english: Keep these things always in mind: What is the nature of the universe, and what is my nature? How do they relate to each other? What kind of part am I in what kind of whole? Remember that no one can stop you from always acting and speaking in ways that fit with the nature you are part of.
original_excerpt: These things thou must always have in mind: What is the nature of the universe, and what is mine--in particular: This unto that what relation it hath: what kind of part, of what kind of universe it is: And that there is nobody that can hinder thee, but that thou mayest always both do and speak those things which are agreeable to that nature, whereof thou art a part.

plain_english: Theophrastus compares different types of wrongdoing. He says the wrongs we commit out of desire are worse than those we commit in anger. When someone acts in anger, they seem to turn away from reason with a kind of pain and inner struggle. But someone who sins from lust is overcome by pleasure. This shows a weaker, less disciplined character. Theophrastus is right to say that the person who sins for pleasure deserves more blame than the one who sins from pain. The angry person might have been wronged first, and grief pushed them to anger. But the person driven by lust chose their action freely.
original_excerpt: Theophrastus, where he compares sin with sin (as after a vulgar sense such things I grant may be compared:) says well and like a philosopher, that those sins are greater which are committed through lust, than those which are committed through anger. For he that is angry seems with a kind of grief and close contraction of himself, to turn away from reason; but he that sins through lust, being overcome by pleasure, doth in his very sin bewray a more impotent, and unmanlike disposition. Well then and like a philosopher doth he say, that he of the two is the more to be condemned, that sins with pleasure, than he that sins with grief. For indeed this latter may seem first to have been wronged, and so in some manner through grief thereof to have been forced to be angry, whereas he who through lust doth commit anything, did of himself merely resolve upon that action.

plain_english: Whatever you want to do, whatever you plan — do it all as someone who might die right now, for all you know.
original_excerpt: Whatsoever thou dost affect, whatsoever thou dost project, so do, and so project all, as one who, for aught thou knowest, may at this very present depart out of this life.

plain_english: As for death, if there are gods, leaving human society is nothing to grieve about. The gods won't harm you — you can be sure of that. But if there are no gods, or if they don't care about the world, why would I want to live in a world empty of gods and divine care? But there are gods, and they do care for the world. As for things that are truly evil — like vice and wickedness — they put those within our own power so we can avoid them if we choose. If there were anything else that was truly bad, they would have made sure we could avoid that too.
original_excerpt: And as for death, if there be any gods, it is no grievous thing to leave the society of men. The gods will do thee no hurt, thou mayest be sure. But if it be so that there be no gods, or that they take no care of the world, why should I desire to live in a world void of gods, and of all divine providence? But gods there be certainly, and they take care for the world; and as for those things which be truly evil, as vice and wickedness, such things they have put in a man's own power, that he might avoid them if he would: and had there been anything besides that had been truly bad and evil, they would have had a care of that also, that a man might have avoided it.

plain_english: Why should we think that things which don't make us better or worse as people can really hurt our lives? We shouldn't think that the universe either doesn't know about these things, or knows about them but can't prevent or arrange them better. The universe doesn't lack power or skill. It wouldn't make such a mistake as to let all things—good and bad—happen randomly to everyone, both good people and bad people alike. Life and death, honor and disgrace, work and pleasure, wealth and poverty—these things do happen to everyone equally. But they are not good or bad in themselves. By themselves, they are neither shameful nor praiseworthy.
original_excerpt: But why should that be thought to hurt and prejudice a man's life in this world, which cannot any ways make man himself the better, or the worse in his own person? Neither must we think that the nature of the universe did either through ignorance pass these things, or if not as ignorant of them, yet as unable either to prevent, or better to order and dispose them. It cannot be that she through want either of power or skill, should have committed such a thing, so as to suffer all things both good and bad, equally and promiscuously, to happen unto all both good and bad. As for life therefore, and death, honour and dishonour, labour and pleasure, riches and poverty, all these things happen unto men indeed, both good and bad, equally; but as things which of themselves are neither good nor bad; because of themselves, neither shameful nor praiseworthy.

plain_english: Think about how quickly everything dissolves and breaks down. Bodies and all physical things return to the basic matter of the world. Even memories fade into the passage of time. Think about the nature of all the things we can see and touch in this world. Look especially at the things that trap us with pleasure, or frighten us because they're painful, or impress us with their shine and status. See how worthless and disgusting they really are. How cheap and rotting. How empty of any real life or meaning.
original_excerpt: Consider how quickly all things are dissolved and resolved: the bodies and substances themselves, into the matter and substance of the world: and their memories into the general age and time of the world.

plain_english: Think about the nature of all the things you can see and touch in this world. Look especially at the things that trap us with pleasure, or frighten us because they seem threatening, or impress us with their shine and status. See how worthless and cheap they really are. How they rot and fall apart. How empty of real life and substance they are.
original_excerpt: Consider the nature of all worldly sensible things; of those especially, which either ensnare by pleasure, or for their irksomeness are dreadful, or for their outward lustre and show are in great esteem and request, how vile and contemptible, how base and corruptible, how destitute of all true life and being they are.

plain_english: Think about how you are connected to God, and through what part of yourself. Think about what happens to that part when it spreads out everywhere. Nothing is more miserable than a soul that circles around all things, searching even the depths of the earth. It tries to guess what other people are thinking through signs and clues. Yet this same soul doesn't realize that it's enough for a person to focus completely on tending the spirit within. Just serve that spirit truly and honestly.
original_excerpt: It is the part of a man endowed with a good understanding faculty, to consider what they themselves are in very deed, from whose bare conceits and voices, honour and credit do proceed: as also what it is to die, and how if a man shall consider this by itself alone, to die, and separate from it in his mind all those things which with it usually represent themselves unto us, he can conceive of it no otherwise, than as of a work of nature, and he that fears any work of nature, is a very child.

plain_english: True service means keeping yourself free from violent emotions and harmful feelings. Stay away from rashness and empty pride, and from all kinds of discontent toward the gods or other people. Whatever comes from the gods deserves respect because of their excellence. Whatever comes from other people should be met with love, since they are our family. Sometimes we should feel pity and compassion too, because they act from ignorance about what is truly good and bad. This blindness is like being unable to tell white from black.
original_excerpt: Now death, it is not only a work of nature, but also conducing to nature.

plain_english:
Even if you lived three thousand years, or ten thousand, remember this: you can only lose the life you're living right now. The life you live is nothing more than what you lose moment by moment.

So the longest life and the shortest life end the same way. The past may seem unequal between people, but the present moment is the same for everyone. And since the present is all we lose when we die, it's clear we only ever lose a single moment.

You can't lose the past or the future. How can you lose what you don't have?
original_excerpt: Consider with thyself how man, and by what part of his, is joined unto God, and how that part of man is affected, when it is said to be diffused. There is nothing more wretched than that soul, which in a kind of circuit compasseth all things, searching (as he saith) even the very depths of the earth; and by all signs and conjectures prying into the very thoughts of other men's souls; and yet of this, is not sensible, that it is sufficient for a man to apply himself wholly, and to confine all his thoughts and cares to the tendance of that spirit which is within him, and truly and really to serve him.

plain_english: Remember two things. First, everything in the world has been the same forever. The same patterns repeat endlessly. So it doesn't matter much if you see these things for a hundred years or two hundred years or forever. They're always the same. Second, the life that the longest-lived person loses at death is exactly the same length as the life the shortest-lived person loses. Because the only thing either person actually has is the present moment. That's the only thing they can lose. You can't lose what you never had.
original_excerpt: His service doth consist in this, that a man keep himself pure from all violent passion and evil affection, from all rashness and vanity, and from all manner of discontent, either in regard of the gods or men. For indeed whatsoever proceeds from the gods, deserves respect for their worth and excellency; and whatsoever proceeds from men, as they are our kinsmen, should by us be entertained, with love, always; sometimes, as proceeding from their ignorance, of that which is truly good and bad, (a blindness no less, than that by which we are not able to discern between white and black:) with a kind of pity and compassion also.

plain_english: Remember that everything is just opinion and imagination. This truth was clear to Monimus the Cynic, and it's clear how useful this insight can be — if you accept what is true and serious about it, not just what sounds pleasant.
original_excerpt: If thou shouldst live three thousand, or as many as ten thousands of years, yet remember this, that man can part with no life properly, save with that little part of life, which he now lives: and that which he lives, is no other, than that which at every instant he parts with. That then which is longest of duration, and that which is shortest, come both to one effect. For although in regard of that which is already past there may be some inequality, yet that time which is now present and in being, is equal unto all men. And that being it which we part with whensoever we die, it doth manifestly appear, that it can be but a moment of time, that we then part with. For as for that which is either past or to come, a man cannot be said properly to part with it. For how should a man part with that which he hath not?

plain_english: A person's soul wrongs itself in several ways. First and worst, when it becomes like a tumor on the world — when it gets upset about things that happen. Being angry at events goes against the nature of the universe, which we are all part of. Second, when it turns against another person or harbors feelings that would harm them — like people who stay angry do. Third, when it gets overwhelmed by pleasure or pain. Fourth, when it lies or acts fake. Fifth, when it acts without purpose, rushing into things without thinking about how they fit the bigger picture. Even small actions should serve a purpose. And the purpose of thinking beings is to follow the reason and law that governs this great city we all live in.
original_excerpt: These two things therefore thou must remember. First, that all things in the world from all eternity, by a perpetual revolution of the same times and things ever continued and renewed, are of one kind and nature; so that whether for a hundred or two hundred years only, or for an infinite space of time, a man see those things which are still the same, it can be no matter of great moment. And secondly, that that life which any the longest liver, or the shortest liver parts with, is for length and duration the very same, for that only which is present, is that, which either of them can lose, as being that only which they have; for that which he hath not, no man can truly be said to lose.

plain_english: A man's life is just a dot in time. Everything about it keeps changing, our senses deceive us, and our bodies decay. The soul is restless, luck is unpredictable, and fame means nothing. In short, everything physical flows like a stream. Everything mental drifts like a dream or smoke. Life is war and wandering. Fame after death is just another kind of forgetting. What can you hold onto then? Only one thing: philosophy. And philosophy means this: protect the spirit inside you from insults and harm, from both pain and pleasure. Never act rashly or fake or hypocritically. Depend completely on yourself and your own actions. Accept whatever happens to you gladly, since it comes from the same source you came from. And above all, wait for death calmly and cheerfully. Death is just the breaking apart of the elements that make up every living thing. If the elements themselves don't suffer when they constantly change into each other, why should anyone fear this dissolution and change that happens to everyone? Isn't this natural? And nothing natural can be evil.
original_excerpt: Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic; and as plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if that which is true and serious in them, be received as well as that which is sweet and pleasing.

plain_english: A person's soul wrongs itself in several ways. First, when it becomes like a tumor or growth on the world — when it gets upset about things that happen. Being grieved by what happens goes against the nature of the universe. We are all part of that nature. Second, when it turns against another person or is driven by desires that hurt others — like angry people do. Third, when it gets overwhelmed by pleasure or pain. Fourth, when it lies or pretends, saying or doing things falsely. Fifth, when it acts without a clear purpose, rushing ahead without thinking about whether its actions fit with the greater good. Even small things should be done with purpose. The purpose of thinking beings is to follow the reason and law that governs this great city and ancient community we all belong to.
original_excerpt: A man's soul doth wrong and disrespect itself first and especially, when as much as in itself lies it becomes an aposteme, and as it were an excrescency of the world, for to be grieved and displeased with anything that happens in the world, is direct apostacy from the nature of the universe; part of which, all particular natures of the world, are. Secondly, when she either is averse from any man, or led by contrary desires or affections, tending to his hurt and prejudice; such as are the souls of them that are angry. Thirdly, when she is overcome by any pleasure or pain. Fourthly, when she doth dissemble, and covertly and falsely either doth or saith anything. Fifthly, when she doth either affect or endeavour anything to no certain end, but rashly and without due ratiocination and consideration, how consequent or inconsequent it is to the common end. For even the least things ought not to be done, without relation unto the end; and the end of the reasonable creatures is, to follow and obey him, who is the reason as it were, and the law of this great city, and ancient commonwealth.

plain_english: A man's life is just a point in time. Everything about it flows away. Our senses are dim, and our bodies decay. The soul is restless. Fortune shifts. Fame means nothing. In short, everything about the body flows like a stream. Everything about the soul passes like a dream or smoke. Life is a battle and a journey. Fame after death is the same as being forgotten. What stays with us then? Only one thing: philosophy. Philosophy means protecting the spirit inside you from all insults and harm. It means rising above pain and pleasure. Never act rashly or fake or hypocritically. Depend entirely on yourself and your own actions. Accept whatever happens as coming from the same source you came from. Above all, wait for death with gentleness and calm joy. Death is just the breaking apart of the elements that make up every living thing. If the elements don't suffer when they constantly change into each other, why should we fear this common dissolution and change? This is how nature works. Nothing that follows nature can be evil.
original_excerpt: The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body tending to corruption. His soul is restless, fortune uncertain, and fame doubtful; to be brief, as a stream so are all things belonging to the body; as a dream, or as a smoke, so are all that belong unto the soul. Our life is a warfare, and a mere pilgrimage. Fame after life is no better than oblivion. What is it then that will adhere and follow? Only one thing, philosophy. And philosophy doth consist in this, for a man to preserve that spirit which is within him, from all manner of contumelies and injuries, and above all pains or pleasures; never to do anything either rashly, or feignedly, or hypocritically: wholly to depend from himself and his own proper actions: all things that happen unto him to embrace contentedly, as coming from Him from whom he himself also came; and above all things, with all meekness and a calm cheerfulness, to expect death, as being nothing else but the resolution of those elements, of which every creature is composed. And if the elements themselves suffer nothing by this their perpetual conversion of one into another, that dissolution, and alteration, which is so common unto all, why should it be feared by any? Is not this according to nature? But nothing that is according to nature can be evil.
